cases.html:
A folder of plain Markdown files is the easiest notes format for a coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex, because the agent already knows how to work with files: it lists a directory, searches with grep, reads a file and edits it. There is no API, no export step and no sync token to set up. The sensible way to start is to give the agent a copy of the folder, or a folder under git, ask it to read first, and review what it changed with a diff before you keep it.

Why plain files suit agents

Coding agents are built around a working directory. The tools they reach for are the ones developers use every day: list files, search text, open a file, write a file, run a command. A notes folder fits that loop without translation.

  • Reading is cheap. grep -rn "pricing" . finds every note that mentions pricing, with the line. The agent does not need a database client or a search endpoint, and it can read only the three files that matter instead of the whole library.
  • Writing is a file write. Appending a section to Project plan.md is the same operation as editing source code. Nothing has to be re-imported afterwards.
  • Structure is already text. Headings, lists, tables, front matter and [[wikilinks]] are all characters in a file, so an agent can see them and keep them intact. See Markdown front matter for the metadata block at the top of a note.
  • Changes can be reviewed. A text file has a line diff. With git, or even diff -r against a copy, you can see exactly which lines an agent touched.

Notes locked in an app database usually need an export, a vendor API or a plugin before an agent can read them. This is the same argument local-first Markdown notes make for people: the files outlive the app, and the agent is one more tool that benefits.

Point an agent at the folder safely

An agent with file access can change files. That is the feature, and it is also the risk, so set it up in a way that makes every change visible and reversible.

1. Work on a copy first

Before the first session, copy the library somewhere else and point the agent at the copy:

cp -R ~/Notes ~/Notes-agent-test
cd ~/Notes-agent-test

Run your agent from that directory. If something goes wrong, delete the copy. Once you trust a type of task, you can move to the real folder.

2. Put the real folder under git

If the folder is not a repository yet, make it one before an agent touches it:

cd ~/Notes
git init
git add -A
git commit -m "notes before agent session"

Now git status shows which files an agent changed, git diff shows the lines, and git restore <file> or git checkout -- . puts a note back. Commit again after you have reviewed the diff and are happy with it.

3. Ask for read-only work first

Start with tasks that should not write anything: "summarize the notes tagged project-x", "list notes that mention a contract but have no date in the front matter", "find notes that link to a title that does not exist". If the answers are useful, move on to edits. When you do ask for edits, name the files, and say what must stay unchanged, such as front matter, code fences and links.

4. Know what an agent can break

  • Front matter. A careless rewrite can reformat or drop the YAML block at the top of a note.
  • Links. Renaming a file or changing a heading can break [[wikilinks]] and anchors that point to it, and the agent will not see backlinks unless it searches for them.
  • Fences and tables. An unclosed code fence swallows the rest of the note in the preview, and a table with a mismatched header and divider row stops being a table.
  • Attachments. Moving a note without its images leaves broken image paths.
  • Many files at once. A "tidy up all my notes" request is a bulk edit that is hard to review, so ask for one folder at a time.

What MiaoYan gives an agent at V4.11.0

MiaoYan stores each note as a .md file in the folder you choose, so the folder above is simply your library. Two pieces in the open-source repository help an agent.

The miao command

miao is a Bash script that lists, searches, prints, opens and creates notes. Besides help, its commands are list [folder], search <query>, open <title|path>, cat <title|path>, new <title> [text] and update. None of them edits an existing note, so an agent edits the file directly. How the CLI finds your library, with examples, is in Markdown notes from the terminal with the miao CLI.

The MiaoYan Agent Skill

The repository ships a skill in skills/miaoyan, with a SKILL.md. The README describes it as a way to teach your agent MiaoYan syntax, attachments, PPT patterns and CLI workflows, and gives this install command:

npx skills add tw93/MiaoYan/skills/miaoyan -g

The skill is a set of instructions, not a plugin that connects to the app. Read at that tag, it tells an agent to:

  • identify whether you want a note, a PPT presentation, note organization or a CLI operation, and keep your language without translating;
  • preserve existing front matter, fenced code, inline code, math, links, wikilinks and attachment paths when editing;
  • fall back to standard GitHub Flavored Markdown when no MiaoYan-specific feature is needed, with tables, task lists, strikethrough and footnotes as supported extensions;
  • link notes with [[Exact title]], without the .md suffix, and use [[Exact title|label]] when it should read differently, but not invent heading or block-reference syntax;
  • keep local images in an i/ folder under the note's folder and reference them as /i/<filename>, not as file:// URLs or absolute paths;
  • use fenced mermaid, plantuml and markmap blocks for diagrams, $...$ and $$...$$ for math, GitHub alert markers such as > [!NOTE] for callouts, and <details> for collapsible sections;
  • separate slides with a standalone --- line, and never use --- as a plain rule inside a slide;
  • use only the real miao commands, not invent miao edit or miao append, run miao update only when you ask for it, set MIAOYAN_PATH if the CLI cannot find the library, and never guess a private folder or write outside the library you approved;
  • finish by checking for closed fences, valid paths, exact wikilink targets and standalone PPT separators.

Next to SKILL.md, skills/miaoyan/agents/openai.yaml holds a display name, a short description and a default prompt for the skill.

Claude Code's own documentation describes skills as a SKILL.md with YAML front matter inside a skill folder, kept in ~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/ for all projects or .claude/skills/<skill-name>/ inside one repository. Claude uses the description to decide when a skill is relevant, and loads the full body only when it is used.

What happens when the app is open

If an agent edits a note that MiaoYan is showing, the app watches the folder and reloads the file from disk. If the text in your editor differs from the file at that moment, MiaoYan first writes your version to a hidden .miaoyan-conflicts folder in the library root, shows a toast saying "Changed on disk. Your version was backed up", and then loads the disk version.

The practical habit is simple: do not type in a note while an agent is rewriting it, and switch to a different note first. MiaoYan also keeps earlier versions of notes as a safety net, covered in Markdown note version history, but those snapshots live in the app's support folder, not in your notes folder, so git is still the history you control.

What goes wrong

  • The agent writes outside the library. Run it from the notes directory, and for the CLI set MIAOYAN_PATH explicitly rather than letting a script guess.
  • Duplicate titles. miao cat and miao open resolve an exact title to the first match, so give the agent a path such as Projects/Plan when titles repeat.
  • A rewrite changed more than you asked. Run git diff, restore the file, and repeat with a narrower instruction.
  • Sensitive notes. Anything the agent reads becomes part of the session, so keep private notes in a folder you do not point an agent at.

FAQ

Can Claude Code or Codex read my notes without any plugin?

Yes, if they can open the folder. Markdown notes are ordinary files, so file tools and grep are enough. The MiaoYan skill only adds knowledge of the app's syntax and CLI.

Should I give an agent my whole notes folder?

Not at first. Start with a copy or a git repository, read-only tasks and one folder at a time.

On macOS Tahoe and later, Apple Notes can save a note as a Markdown file. Open the note, choose File, then Export To, and pick Markdown. Apple's archive article for iCloud data, published 14 September 2026, says that menu may read Export To or Export as, and that on macOS Sequoia and earlier the File menu only offers Export as PDF. The .md file is plain text. MiaoYan does not open the Notes database. It lists .md, .markdown and .txt files in a folder you pick, and the preview shows only the syntax that is actually in those files.

Export a note on macOS Tahoe

Apple announced this with macOS Tahoe 26. The June 2025 newsroom post says Notes adds the ability to import and export a note into a markdown file, and the September 2025 feature list describes it as saving notes as Markdown files, or importing Markdown formatted files.

The current Notes User Guide on the Mac gives the steps.

  1. Open Notes.
  2. Click the note you want to export.
  3. Choose File > Export To, then choose Markdown. If the menu reads Export as instead, that is the other label in Apple's archive article. Choose Markdown there.
  4. Type a name if you want a different file name, and add Finder tags if you want them searchable in Finder.
  5. Click Save.

The same guide has a second path for a fragment of the note. Select the text in the note body, then choose Edit > Copy as Markdown, and paste it into a new .md file. Pasting Markdown back into Notes turns it into formatted headings, lists, and similar rich text. That direction is useful when you are checking a file you already wrote.

On iPhone, the current user guide says to open the note, tap the share button, then tap Export as Markdown. If that option is missing, tap the View More button first, then choose how to send or save the note. The iOS 18 edition of that page has PDF, Pages, and print, and it stops there. Importing a .md file into Notes, the other direction, is documented for macOS Tahoe 26, iOS 26, and iPadOS 26 and later. On the Mac the menu is File > Import Markdown, and the notes land in a folder named Imported Notes.

The export steps describe one note. They do not describe a command that exports a Notes folder. Import is the place Apple documents a folder: File > Import to Notes can take a folder, and Preserve folder structure on import keeps that layout. The checkbox sits behind Options, or Show Options, when it is hidden. For export, you pick the destination yourself, so the folder the .md file lands in is the one you chose in the save dialog.

What Sequoia and earlier can do

The Notes User Guide for macOS 15 says you can export a note as a PDF with File > Export as PDF, or open it in Pages with File > Open in Pages. The Pages document keeps formatting such as bullets, indentation, and bold text, and it is a separate copy. Changes in Notes do not flow back to that Pages file. That guide's export page has PDF and Pages, and no Markdown command.

A short note is often faster to write again in Markdown than to push through a converter. When you want the drawings, scans, tables, and photos as files, Obsidian's Importer plugin documents a different route, and it does not use Apple's Markdown menu. It reads the Notes data on macOS. In Obsidian, open Settings, install Importer from Community Plugins, enable it, open it, set File format to Apple Notes, and choose Import. The open panel is titled Select the "group.com.apple.notes" folder to allow Obsidian to read Apple Notes data. Review the generated template and the preview, then select Import again. Obsidian's help says this covers tables, images, drawings, scans, PDFs, and links introduced in iOS 17. Locked notes are skipped until you unlock them, because Apple encrypts them. Scans come out as uncropped images, cropped images, or PDFs, depending on which system created or edited them. The plugin runs on macOS, and the iOS app does not have it yet. The folder it writes is ordinary Markdown, which is what you then point MiaoYan at. What happens to Obsidian-only syntax after that is covered in an Obsidian alternative for Mac.

On iPhone, Open in Pages shows which objects are fragile even when Markdown is available. The current iPhone guide says you cannot edit drawings in Pages, scans and PDFs show up as thumbnails, and tags, mentions, checklists, and links to other notes are not active items there. A PDF export uses the note's current attachment view, and a multipage PDF or scan contributes only its first page. That is a description of Pages and PDF, not a Markdown specification. It is still the reason a text export has to flatten or drop some of those objects.

Why the preview follows the file

Notes stores a rich-text note. Markdown is a text file whose meaning comes from characters such as #, -, and |. Apple's export pages name the command and the file type. They do not publish a map of what a checklist, a table, an attachment, or a drawing becomes. Open the .md file as text and read it.

MiaoYan parses that text with cmark-gfm. The extensions it turns on are table, footnotes, strikethrough, tasklist, and autolink. A checklist displays as a checkbox when the line is a task item, written - [ ] for an open item or - [x] for a done one. A grid displays as a table when the file contains a GFM table, with a header row and a divider row. The syntax, including the divider mistakes that leave a table as plain text, is in the Markdown cheat sheet. A drawing, a scan, or a PDF shows up when the export wrote a file and the note links to it. If the .md file has a sentence where the drawing was, the preview has nothing else to draw.

Images are the part that usually needs a path fix. When MiaoYan saves an image you paste, it writes the file into an i directory in the folder that contains the note, and inserts a link of the form ![](/i/filename). Other files go under files and use a /files/ prefix. The preview resolves /i/... against that same folder. A relative path with no leading slash, such as attachments/photo.png, is resolved against that folder too. A path that starts with / and is not /i/ is treated as an absolute path on disk, so an image link /files/photo.png looks for a file at /files/photo.png in the preview, rather than inside your notes folder.

GitHub reads the same characters differently. Its documentation says a link is relative to the current file, and a link that starts with / is relative to the repository root. A MiaoYan /i/photo.png link finds the image beside the note in MiaoYan. On GitHub it looks for i/photo.png at the root of the repository. If these notes will also be read on GitHub, a relative link such as i/photo.png or attachments/photo.png points at the same file in both, as long as the image sits where that path says, next to the note.

Put the files in a folder MiaoYan opens

If you already keep notes in a folder, as described in local-first Markdown notes, copy the exported .md files into it, and copy the image files so each link still names a real file. MiaoYan watches the folder with macOS file system events and adds a new .md, .markdown, or .txt file to the list. That copy does not need a restart.

If this export should be the library, set it as the note location. Choose MiaoYan > Preferences… (Command-,), stay on General, and click Change next to Note Location. Pick the folder. MiaoYan checks that it is a writable directory. When the check fails, the alert title is "Could not use this folder", and the old location stays. The message under that title says whether the folder could not be read or written, and for a cloud drive it suggests opening that drive's app to make sure the folder shows in Finder, or enabling offline access. After a valid choice, MiaoYan saves the folder at once and shows a "Restart" button in the row, since the new folder is used from the next start. Syncing that folder with iCloud Drive or another service is a separate decision, covered in syncing Markdown notes across devices.

A layout that matches the images MiaoYan writes itself looks like this:

Inbox/
  Meeting notes.md
  i/
    photo.png

The note then contains ![photo](/i/photo.png). The sidebar skips folders named i, files, assets, .cache, and .Trash. It also hides a folder that holds only attachment files, with no notes and no subfolders. Those files stay on disk. If the export arrived as a Markdown file plus a folder of pictures, and the pictures are absent from the sidebar, that rule is what hid the folder.

The title in the list is the file name without the extension. Rename the file in Finder when the save dialog left a name you do not want. The note you open is that file.

Check what came across

Open the .md file in any text editor before you judge the preview. Search for ![ to see image links, for - [ to see whether a checklist became a task list, and for a row of pipes and dashes to see whether a table became a GFM table. When those strings are absent, the preview has no checkbox, table, or picture to build.

Then confirm the files. In MiaoYan, Reveal in Finder (Option-Command-R) shows the note file. In Finder, the image named in the link should sit at that path relative to the note's folder, or under i if you rewrote the link to /i/. Toggle Preview with Command-3. A missing local image is replaced in the preview by a small box whose text reads "Image Not Found". Toggle Split View with Command-backslash when you want the source and the preview together.

A note missing from the list is usually a file the app did not treat as a note. The extension has to be md, markdown, or txt, matched without regard to case, so .MD is listed too. The file has to be under 100,000,000 bytes, and its type has to be text or Markdown. Hidden files are skipped, and so are files inside i, files, or an assets folder with no notes in it. If you changed Note Location and have not restarted yet, the app is still reading the previous folder.

When a text file is the wrong copy

A sketch, a marked-up PDF, or a scan you still need as a document fits a PDF better than a text file. Apple's PDF export is the documented visual copy, with the first-page limit on iPhone for a multipage PDF or scan. Obsidian's importer is the documented way, on a Mac, to pull tables, images, drawings, scans, and PDFs out of the Notes store in one pass. MiaoYan is where you open the resulting folder when you want to keep editing those files as Markdown. A drawing that the .md file does not link to an image stays absent in the preview.

FAQ

Can one command export a whole Notes folder?

The Mac user guide describes clicking one note and choosing File > Export To. Import is the command that can take a folder and keep its structure. A library-wide conversion on the Mac is what Obsidian's Importer documents, by reading the Notes data folder.

Does a checked item stay checked?

It stays checked when the exported line is - [x]. An open item is - [ ]. A circle character or a plain sentence stays plain text in the preview. The cheat sheet covers how a click in MiaoYan's preview writes the checkbox back into the file.

Why does the same image link work in one app and miss in the other?

/i/photo.png points at the i folder beside the note in MiaoYan. On GitHub, a link that starts with / points at the repository root, which is a different directory unless the notes folder is the root of the repo. A relative path such as i/photo.png or attachments/photo.png names the same file in both when the image sits at that path next to the note.

Does copying files in require a restart?

Copying into the folder that is already the note location does not. The file watcher imports the new note. Restart belongs to a change of Note Location.

On iPhone, the current user guide says to open the note, tap the share button, then tap Export as Markdown. If that option is missing, tap the View More button first, then choose how to send or save the note. The iOS 18 edition of that page has PDF, Pages, and print, and it stops there. Importing a `.md` file into Notes, the other direction, is documented for macOS Tahoe 26, iOS 26, and iPadOS 26 and later. On the Mac the menu is File > Import Markdown, and the notes land in a folder named Imported Notes.

The export steps describe one note. They do not describe a command that exports a Notes folder. Import is the place Apple documents a folder: File > Import to Notes can take a folder, and Preserve folder structure on import keeps that layout. The checkbox sits behind Options, or Show Options, when it is hidden. For export, you pick the destination yourself, so the folder the `.md` file lands in is the one you chose in the save dialog.

## What Sequoia and earlier can do

The Notes User Guide for macOS 15 says you can export a note as a PDF with File > Export as PDF, or open it in Pages with File > Open in Pages. The Pages document keeps formatting such as bullets, indentation, and bold text, and it is a separate copy. Changes in Notes do not flow back to that Pages file. That guide's export page has PDF and Pages, and no Markdown command.

A short note is often faster to write again in Markdown than to push through a converter. When you want the drawings, scans, tables, and photos as files, Obsidian's Importer plugin documents a different route, and it does not use Apple's Markdown menu. It reads the Notes data on macOS. In Obsidian, open Settings, install Importer from Community Plugins, enable it, open it, set File format to Apple Notes, and choose Import. The open panel is titled Select the "group.com.apple.notes" folder to allow Obsidian to read Apple Notes data. Review the generated template and the preview, then select Import again. Obsidian's help says this covers tables, images, drawings, scans, PDFs, and links introduced in iOS 17. Locked notes are skipped until you unlock them, because Apple encrypts them. Scans come out as uncropped images, cropped images, or PDFs, depending on which system created or edited them. The plugin runs on macOS, and the iOS app does not have it yet. The folder it writes is ordinary Markdown, which is what you then point MiaoYan at. What happens to Obsidian-only syntax after that is covered in [an Obsidian alternative for Mac](/blog/obsidian-alternative-mac/).

On iPhone, Open in Pages shows which objects are fragile even when Markdown is available. The current iPhone guide says you cannot edit drawings in Pages, scans and PDFs show up as thumbnails, and tags, mentions, checklists, and links to other notes are not active items there. A PDF export uses the note's current attachment view, and a multipage PDF or scan contributes only its first page. That is a description of Pages and PDF, not a Markdown specification. It is still the reason a text export has to flatten or drop some of those objects.

## Why the preview follows the file

Notes stores a rich-text note. Markdown is a text file whose meaning comes from characters such as `#`, `-`, and `|`. Apple's export pages name the command and the file type. They do not publish a map of what a checklist, a table, an attachment, or a drawing becomes. Open the `.md` file as text and read it.

MiaoYan parses that text with cmark-gfm. The extensions it turns on are `table`, `footnotes`, `strikethrough`, `tasklist`, and `autolink`. A checklist displays as a checkbox when the line is a task item, written `- [ ]` for an open item or `- [x]` for a done one. A grid displays as a table when the file contains a GFM table, with a header row and a divider row. The syntax, including the divider mistakes that leave a table as plain text, is in the [Markdown cheat sheet](/blog/markdown-cheat-sheet/). A drawing, a scan, or a PDF shows up when the export wrote a file and the note links to it. If the `.md` file has a sentence where the drawing was, the preview has nothing else to draw.

Images are the part that usually needs a path fix. When MiaoYan saves an image you paste, it writes the file into an `i` directory in the folder that contains the note, and inserts a link of the form `![](/i/filename)`. Other files go under `files` and use a `/files/` prefix. The preview resolves `/i/...` against that same folder. A relative path with no leading slash, such as `attachments/photo.png`, is resolved against that folder too. A path that starts with `/` and is not `/i/` is treated as an absolute path on disk, so an image link `/files/photo.png` looks for a file at `/files/photo.png` in the preview, rather than inside your notes folder.

GitHub reads the same characters differently. Its documentation says a link is relative to the current file, and a link that starts with `/` is relative to the repository root. A MiaoYan `/i/photo.png` link finds the image beside the note in MiaoYan. On GitHub it looks for `i/photo.png` at the root of the repository. If these notes will also be read on GitHub, a relative link such as `i/photo.png` or `attachments/photo.png` points at the same file in both, as long as the image sits where that path says, next to the note.

## Put the files in a folder MiaoYan opens

If you already keep notes in a folder, as described in [local-first Markdown notes](/blog/local-first-markdown-notes/), copy the exported `.md` files into it, and copy the image files so each link still names a real file. MiaoYan watches the folder with macOS file system events and adds a new `.md`, `.markdown`, or `.txt` file to the list. That copy does not need a restart.

If this export should be the library, set it as the note location. Choose MiaoYan > Preferences… (Command-,), stay on General, and click Change next to Note Location. Pick the folder. MiaoYan checks that it is a writable directory. When the check fails, the alert title is "Could not use this folder", and the old location stays. The message under that title says whether the folder could not be read or written, and for a cloud drive it suggests opening that drive's app to make sure the folder shows in Finder, or enabling offline access. After a valid choice, MiaoYan saves the folder at once and shows a "Restart" button in the row, since the new folder is used from the next start. Syncing that folder with iCloud Drive or another service is a separate decision, covered in [syncing Markdown notes across devices](/blog/sync-markdown-notes-across-devices/).

A layout that matches the images MiaoYan writes itself looks like this:

```text
Inbox/
  Meeting notes.md
  i/
    photo.png
```

The note then contains `![photo](/i/photo.png)`. The sidebar skips folders named `i`, `files`, `assets`, `.cache`, and `.Trash`. It also hides a folder that holds only attachment files, with no notes and no subfolders. Those files stay on disk. If the export arrived as a Markdown file plus a folder of pictures, and the pictures are absent from the sidebar, that rule is what hid the folder.

The title in the list is the file name without the extension. Rename the file in Finder when the save dialog left a name you do not want. The note you open is that file.

## Check what came across

Open the `.md` file in any text editor before you judge the preview. Search for `![` to see image links, for `- [` to see whether a checklist became a task list, and for a row of pipes and dashes to see whether a table became a GFM table. When those strings are absent, the preview has no checkbox, table, or picture to build.

Then confirm the files. In MiaoYan, Reveal in Finder (Option-Command-R) shows the note file. In Finder, the image named in the link should sit at that path relative to the note's folder, or under `i` if you rewrote the link to `/i/`. Toggle Preview with Command-3. A missing local image is replaced in the preview by a small box whose text reads "Image Not Found". Toggle Split View with Command-backslash when you want the source and the preview together.

A note missing from the list is usually a file the app did not treat as a note. The extension has to be `md`, `markdown`, or `txt`, matched without regard to case, so `.MD` is listed too. The file has to be under 100,000,000 bytes, and its type has to be text or Markdown. Hidden files are skipped, and so are files inside `i`, `files`, or an `assets` folder with no notes in it. If you changed Note Location and have not restarted yet, the app is still reading the previous folder.

## When a text file is the wrong copy

A sketch, a marked-up PDF, or a scan you still need as a document fits a PDF better than a text file. Apple's PDF export is the documented visual copy, with the first-page limit on iPhone for a multipage PDF or scan. Obsidian's importer is the documented way, on a Mac, to pull tables, images, drawings, scans, and PDFs out of the Notes store in one pass. MiaoYan is where you open the resulting folder when you want to keep editing those files as Markdown. A drawing that the `.md` file does not link to an image stays absent in the preview.

## FAQ

### Can one command export a whole Notes folder?

The Mac user guide describes clicking one note and choosing File > Export To. Import is the command that can take a folder and keep its structure. A library-wide conversion on the Mac is what Obsidian's Importer documents, by reading the Notes data folder.

### Does a checked item stay checked?

It stays checked when the exported line is `- [x]`. An open item is `- [ ]`. A circle character or a plain sentence stays plain text in the preview. The cheat sheet covers how a click in MiaoYan's preview writes the checkbox back into the file.

### Why does the same image link work in one app and miss in the other?

`/i/photo.png` points at the `i` folder beside the note in MiaoYan. On GitHub, a link that starts with `/` points at the repository root, which is a different directory unless the notes folder is the root of the repo. A relative path such as `i/photo.png` or `attachments/photo.png` names the same file in both when the image sits at that path next to the note.

### Does copying files in require a restart?

Copying into the folder that is already the note location does not. The file watcher imports the new note. Restart belongs to a change of Note Location.

cases.html:
If you want to leave Bear but keep writing Markdown on a Mac, the move is to export your notes as .md files and open the folder in an editor that reads plain files. MiaoYan does this: folders are your categories, every note is a file, and an iCloud Drive folder carries the notes to iPhone and iPad. Bear organizes with tags across the whole library and MiaoYan has no tags at all, so a library that lives on #tags needs a plan before you move.

What Bear does well

Bear's own FAQ describes tags as working like hashtags: type #tag anywhere in a note, put as many tags on a note as you like, wrap a phrase in pound signs for a multi-word tag (#vacation plans#), and nest them with a slash (#recipes/italian). Click a tag in the sidebar and you see every note that contains it. That is a different model from folders, because one note can sit under several tags at once.

The editor is built on the CommonMark specification, and its Markdown guide says formatting is displayed while the note stays plain text, with a "Hide Markdown" setting under Settings > General. It runs on Mac and iOS, and Bear Web works in any major browser with the same iCloud credentials.

Sync is a Pro feature. Bear's Pro page lists iCloud sync, note encryption, export to PDF, HTML, DOCX and JPG, themes and OCR search, at $2.99 a month or $29.99 a year with a 7-day trial (page checked on 2026-10-19; prices change, so confirm on Bear's page). The sync page says Bear syncs through CloudKit, not through files in iCloud Drive.

How Bear stores your notes

Bear keeps notes in a SQLite database on iOS and macOS. On a Mac it sits at ~/Library/Group Containers/9K33E3U3T4.net.shinyfrog.bear/Application Data/database.sqlite. Bear's own page says it is safe to access the database for reading only, advises most users not to edit it, and asks anyone who does to make a copy and quit Bear first.

That is the main difference from a folder of files. A Bear note is not a file you can see in Finder or search with grep. The notes are still yours, but you get them out through Bear's export, not by copying a file.

Get your notes out of Bear

The free version of Bear exports to Plain Text, Markdown (.md), Text Bundle, Bear Note and RTF. HTML, DOCX, PDF, JPEG and ePub need Pro, but you do not need them for this move.

  1. In Bear for Mac, click "Notes" in the sidebar and press ⌘A.
  2. Choose File > Export notes… (⇧⌘S) and pick Markdown.
  3. Save into a new, empty folder, for example ~/Documents/BearExport.
  4. In Bear > Preferences > General, check "Keep tags during export" before you export if you want tags kept in the files.

Bear's export page does not say how attachments are laid out for each format, so open the folder and check a note with an image before you trust it. If images are missing, export a second time in Text Bundle and compare the two.

Move them into MiaoYan

MiaoYan reads a folder of .md, .markdown or .txt files, so the import is a folder choice.

  1. Copy the export folder to where you want the library, for example a MiaoYan folder in iCloud Drive.
  2. Open Preferences with ⌘, and find "Note Location".
  3. Click "Change", choose the folder, and click "Restart" when it appears in the row. MiaoYan loads the library at launch.

Sub-folders become sidebar folders. Bear had no folders, so your export is probably one flat list. Make a handful of folders by hand and drag notes in, sorted by the thing that used to be your top-level tag. MiaoYan reads relative image paths from the note's folder and saves its own pasted images as ![name](/i/name.png) in an i/ folder there, so open a few notes with images after the move and fix any links that do not resolve. The Obsidian migration post shows the same kind of cleanup with rg.

How MiaoYan's model differs

MiaoYan treats the folder tree as the only structure. A note lives in exactly one folder, its title is the file name, and nothing is stored outside the files except version snapshots in the app's support folder. Links between notes use [[Title]] wikilinks with backlinks, covered in Wikilinks and backlinks. Bear can link notes too, and its export page mentions an "HTML Links" option that turns wiki links into HTML links, so these are worth checking after export.

For the iPhone and iPad, MiaoYan has no account and no sync service of its own. The apps open the same iCloud Drive folder as the Mac, and iCloud moves the files. Sync Markdown notes across devices covers the failure cases.

What Bear does better, and what you lose

  • Tags across folders. MiaoYan has none. You can type #recipes as text and search for it, but it is only text.
  • A mobile app built for writing. Bear has native iPhone and iPad apps, and its FAQ documents iPadOS keyboard shortcuts. MiaoYan's iPhone and iPad app opens a note in a reader first and switches to an editor when you tap the edit button; with a hardware keyboard it has had its own shortcuts since V4.9.0, such as ⌘T for a task, ⌘K for a link, and ⌘] and ⌘[ to shift lines.
  • Apple Watch. Bear's FAQ lists a Watch app, and MiaoYan has none. Widgets and Shortcuts are no longer a gap: since 4.11.0 MiaoYan's iPhone and iPad app has Recent Notes widgets for the Home Screen and Lock Screen, a New Note button for the Lock Screen and Control Center, and Shortcuts and Siri actions that create, open, search and append to notes.
  • Export to PDF, DOCX and JPG as Pro features. MiaoYan has its own PDF route, described in Markdown to PDF on Mac, without DOCX.
  • One note, several places. A note lives in one folder, so it cannot also sit under a second heading.

What you gain is a library that survives any app. Files open in any editor, a backup is a copy of a folder, and there is no Pro tier gating sync, because the sync is whatever you already use for the folder. MiaoYan also renders LaTeX, Mermaid, PlantUML and Markmap on the Mac, which Bear's Markdown guide does not mention.

When to stay with Bear

Stay if tags are how you find things, if you capture mostly on an iPhone, or if you like the styled single-pane editor. If you want a folder-based Mac editor, or want to try plain files before deciding, Choosing a Markdown editor for Mac compares the main options, and Local-first Markdown notes explains why a plain folder is worth the trade.

You can test the move safely: export is non-destructive, so keep Bear installed, export once, open the copy in MiaoYan and use both for a week.

FAQ

Can Bear export all notes to Markdown for free?

Yes. The free version exports to Markdown, plain text, Text Bundle, Bear Note and RTF. Select all notes and use File > Export notes… (⇧⌘S).

Does MiaoYan support Bear's #tags?

No. A #tag in a note stays as text. Folders are the only organization, so turn your main tags into folders before or after the move.

Can I read Bear's database directly?

On a Mac you can open the SQLite file read-only, which Bear says is safe. Export is the supported route, and iOS does not expose the database.

Will my notes sync to iPhone and iPad after the move?

If the library folder is in iCloud Drive, yes. The MiaoYan apps for iPhone and iPad open the same folder, and iCloud does the syncing.

Chinese writers usually put one ordinary space between Han characters and Latin letters or digits, so it is written 使用 Swift 开发 and 第 3 章, not 使用Swift开发. Chinese has no spaces between words, so the space is not a grammar rule; it is a readability convention from the Chinese copywriting guide, and it is not part of Markdown. Markdown passes the characters through unchanged. In MiaoYan two commands in the Edit menu add the spaces: Clean Typography, which has no shortcut and also fixes Chinese punctuation, and Format on ⌘⇧L, which adds them as a side effect of its bundled Prettier formatter.

Why the space exists

Han characters are square and evenly spaced, Latin letters are narrow and proportional, and when the two touch the text looks cramped. Typesetters have long solved this with a small gap, not a full space. The W3C requirements document for Chinese layout, clreq, says that for horizontal text there is, in principle, tracking or spacing of up to a quarter of a Han character's width between a Han character and an adjacent Western letter or numeral, except at the start or end of a line.

Plain text has no such gap, so writers type a real space instead. The best-known statement of the habit is the Chinese Copywriting Guidelines (中文文案排版指北), which asks for a space between Chinese and English, between Chinese and digits, and between digits and units. Its own example is "在 LeanCloud 上，数据存储是围绕 AVObject 进行的", where the inline code gets the same treatment as a Latin word.

The guide is a style convention, not a standard, and plenty of published Chinese text ignores it. What matters for a note is consistency. A mixed archive, with some notes spaced and some not, is the thing that hurts search and diff, because Swift开发 and Swift 开发 are different strings.

The exceptions that matter

Three cases from the guide come up constantly.

  • Full-width punctuation takes no space on either side. Write 刚刚买了一部 iPhone，好开心！, not iPhone ，好开心. The comma, period and question mark already have their own built-in whitespace.
  • Degrees and percent signs attach to the number: 90°, 15%. A space before % is wrong in the guide. Other units do get a space: 10 Gbps, 20 TB.
  • Product names are written as the owner writes them. The guide's example is 豆瓣FM, which is officially written without a space.

Two more cases come from Markdown itself rather than from the guide. Inside code spans and fenced code blocks you must not change anything, because a space is data there. And inside URLs, file paths, link targets and wikilink titles a stray space breaks the link.

What MiaoYan does

MiaoYan has two commands in the Edit menu that both change spacing, and they do different amounts of work.

Format (⌘⇧L, Chinese UI: 文档排版) runs a bundled Prettier Markdown formatter over the note and tidies Markdown structure such as list markers and table alignment. The Prettier it bundles is from the 2.x line, which still inserts a space between Chinese and Latin letters or digits, so 使用Swift开发 comes out as 使用 Swift 开发 here too; Prettier 3.0 dropped that behavior. Format does nothing else for Chinese text: 你好,世界 keeps its half-width comma, a space before a full-width comma stays, and inline code gets no space around it.

Clean Typography (Chinese UI: 清理排版) is the command built for Chinese text. It has no keyboard shortcut. It rewrites the whole open note in one step, and the rewrite lands in the undo stack, so ⌘Z reverts it. If nothing needs changing, it shows a message that the typography is already clean. Like Format, it refuses to run in preview mode, so leave preview first.

The rules in the source are these:

  • A space is inserted between a Han or kana character and an ASCII letter or digit, in either order. 使用Swift开发 becomes 使用 Swift 开发 and 第3章共10节 becomes 第 3 章共 10 节. Existing spacing is left alone.
  • Half-width , ; : ! ? . directly after a Han character becomes the full-width form when it ends a clause, so 你好,世界 becomes 你好，世界. Decimal points and times such as 3.5 and 10:00 are untouched.
  • Spaces next to full-width punctuation are removed.
  • Full-width letters and digits become ASCII, 等等... becomes 等等……, and a single em dash between Han characters becomes a comma. A doubled em dash, the proper Chinese dash, is kept.
  • Runs of blank lines collapse to one.

It does not insert a space between a digit and a Latin unit, so 10Gbps stays as it is, and 90° and 15% are untouched because those symbols are not letters or digits. It also does not know product names such as 豆瓣FM, so review the result.

For text outside MiaoYan, such as a post you are about to send, the Chinese typography cleaner on this site runs the same rules in the browser and marks every change.

What it leaves alone

The cleaner splits each line into protected and plain segments before touching anything. Protected: fenced code (backticks or tildes, including inside block quotes), indented code, inline code, $...$ math and $$ blocks, link and image targets, [[wikilinks]], bare http and https URLs, reference definitions such as [ref]: target and [^1]: note, and front matter. Trailing double spaces, which Markdown reads as a hard line break, are kept.

Chinese writers usually put one ordinary space between Han characters and Latin letters or digits, so it is written `使用 Swift 开发` and `第 3 章`, not `使用Swift开发`. Markdown passes the characters through unchanged. In MiaoYan two commands in the Edit menu add the spaces: Clean Typography, which has no shortcut and also fixes Chinese punctuation, and Format on `⌘⇧L`, which adds them as a side effect of its bundled Prettier formatter.

## Why the space exists

Han characters are square and evenly spaced, Latin letters are narrow and proportional, and when the two touch the text looks cramped. Typesetters have long solved this with a small gap, not a full space. The W3C requirements document for Chinese layout, [clreq](https://www.w3.org/TR/clreq/), says that for horizontal text there is, in principle, tracking or spacing of up to a quarter of a Han character's width between a Han character and an adjacent Western letter or numeral, except at the start or end of a line.

Plain text has no such gap, so writers type a real space instead. The best-known statement of the habit is the [Chinese Copywriting Guidelines](https://github.com/sparanoid/chinese-copywriting-guidelines) (中文文案排版指北), which asks for a space between Chinese and English, between Chinese and digits, and between digits and units. Its own example is "在 LeanCloud 上，数据存储是围绕 `AVObject` 进行的", where the inline code gets the same treatment as a Latin word.

The guide is a style convention, not a standard, and plenty of published Chinese text ignores it. What matters for a note is consistency. A mixed archive, with some notes spaced and some not, is the thing that hurts search and diff, because `Swift开发` and `Swift 开发` are different strings.

## The exceptions that matter

Three cases from the guide come up constantly.

- Full-width punctuation takes no space on either side. Write `刚刚买了一部 iPhone，好开心！`, not `iPhone ，好开心`. The comma, period and question mark already have their own built-in whitespace.
- Degrees and percent signs attach to the number: `90°`, `15%`. A space before `%` is wrong in the guide. Other units do get a space: `10 Gbps`, `20 TB`.
- Product names are written as the owner writes them. The guide's example is 豆瓣FM, which is officially written without a space.

Two more cases come from Markdown itself rather than from the guide. Inside code spans and fenced code blocks you must not change anything, because a space is data there. And inside URLs, file paths, link targets and wikilink titles a stray space breaks the link.

cases.html:
CommonMark is a precise specification of core Markdown, and GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) is a strict superset of it that adds tables, task lists, strikethrough, extended autolinks and a filter for a few dangerous HTML tags. Anything beyond that, such as footnotes, math, callouts and diagrams, is an app feature, not a standard. If you want a note to render the same everywhere, stick to CommonMark plus the GFM extensions you have tested. MiaoYan uses the cmark-gfm parser with five extensions turned on, then adds math, callouts and diagrams in its preview.

Why there are flavors at all

John Gruber released Markdown in 2004 as a syntax description plus a Perl script, Markdown.pl. According to the CommonMark site, the description does not specify the syntax unambiguously, so implementers copied the behavior of Markdown.pl, which was buggy and was last updated in December 2004. By 2014 there were dozens of implementations, and they had drifted apart, and the same file could render differently from one site to the next.

The CommonMark spec fixed that by writing the rules down with examples, and its current version is 0.31.2 (January 2024). The GFM spec is based on CommonMark and says plainly that GFM is a strict superset of it. Its latest published version is 0.29-gfm from April 2019, so it is a snapshot, not a moving target.

This is the whole story of "flavors". There is a core that is now well specified, a small layer of extensions that GitHub standardized, and a long tail where every app does its own thing.

What each layer defines

CommonMark covers headings, emphasis, lists, block quotes, code spans and fences, links, images, raw HTML, hard and soft line breaks, and backslash escapes. A single newline inside a paragraph is a soft break, which renders as a space; a hard break needs a backslash or two trailing spaces at the end of the line.

GFM adds these extensions, each marked as such in its spec:

  • Tables, with a header row and a delimiter row of hyphens, optionally with colons for alignment.
  • Task list items, written - [ ] and - [x].
  • Strikethrough with ~~text~~.
  • Extended autolinks, which turn a bare www.example.com or https://example.com into a link without angle brackets.
  • Disallowed raw HTML, which rewrites the opening < of <title>, <textarea>, <style>, <xmp>, <iframe>, <noembed>, <noframes>, <script> and <plaintext> to < in HTML output.

App extensions are everything else. Footnotes, math with dollar signs, > [!NOTE] callouts, wikilinks and Mermaid diagrams are all common, and none is in the CommonMark or GFM specifications. GitHub itself documents footnotes and alerts on its own syntax page, but those are GitHub features, not part of the published GFM spec.

Which layer MiaoYan implements

MiaoYan renders Markdown with cmark-gfm. In the source, the parser is created with the footnotes option and five extensions attached by name: table, footnotes, strikethrough, tasklist and, since V4.10.0, autolink. The rendering call passes the option that lets raw HTML through. Two things follow:

  • With the autolink extension attached, a bare https://example.com or www.example.com becomes a link in the preview and in exports, as on GitHub. Before V4.10.0 it stayed plain text, so <https://example.com> is still the safer form for notes read in older versions or other apps.
  • The tagfilter extension is not attached, so GFM's disallowed raw HTML rule is not applied in the preview. Raw HTML such as a <details> block renders, which is what makes collapsible sections work, and it also means you should only open notes you trust.

Before the parser runs, MiaoYan shields math. It protects $$ ... $$, $ ... $, \( ... \) and \[ ... \] so that underscores and asterisks in a formula are not read as emphasis; KaTeX typesets them later in the preview. After the parser, a post-processing step turns > [!NOTE], [!TIP], [!IMPORTANT], [!WARNING] and [!CAUTION] blockquotes into callouts, as GitHub does. The preview's script then draws fenced mermaid, plantuml and markmap blocks and colors code with highlight.js. A leading --- front matter block is stripped from the preview when it looks like YAML.

MiaoYan also has a Line Breaks setting with two values, Every Newline and GitHub Style. Under the hood this switches between rendering every newline as a line break and rendering a newline as a space, which is the CommonMark rule. The cheat sheet covers the practical effect.

Wikilinks ([[Project plan]]) are indexed by MiaoYan to build backlinks; see Wikilinks and backlinks. They are not in CommonMark or GFM, so a renderer that does not implement them shows the literal brackets.

Writing portable Markdown

Portable means the file reads well as plain text and renders the same in the apps you actually use. A few habits get most of the way.

  1. Use fenced code blocks with a language word, not indentation.
  2. Put a blank line before and after lists, tables and code fences.
  3. Use - for bullets and a lowercase x in task items.
  4. Write a URL as <https://example.com> or [text](url), never as a bare address.
  5. End a line with a backslash when you need a hard break, since trailing spaces are invisible and often stripped.
  6. Treat footnotes, math, callouts and diagrams as extensions. If the note must be read in a plain viewer, keep the key information outside them.
  7. Avoid raw HTML except where the receiving app is known to allow it.

When a feature is app-specific, decide whether losing it is acceptable. A callout that falls back to a block quote with [!NOTE] in it is fine for a personal note and a poor choice for a README.

A test file for any app

Paste this into a new note in the app you are checking, then compare the preview with the list underneath.

# Heading
Line one
Line two

| a | b |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2 |

- [x] done
- [ ] open

~~struck~~ and www.example.com and <https://example.com>

Footnote[^1]

[^1]: The note.

> [!NOTE]
> A callout.

Inline $a_1 + b_1$ and a block:

$$
x^2 + y^2 = z^2
$$

```mermaid
graph LR
  A --> B
```

Read the result like this. Two lines joined into one means the app follows the CommonMark soft break rule, two lines kept apart means it breaks at every newline. If the table or the task boxes appear as text, the app lacks the GFM extension. The www.example.com link tells you about extended autolinks. A block quote that still shows [!NOTE] has no callouts. Literal dollar signs mean no math, and a code block showing the Mermaid source means no diagrams.

In MiaoYan, expect the table, task boxes and strikethrough to render, www.example.com to stay plain text, the footnote, callout, math and diagram to render, and the two lines to join or separate depending on the Line Break setting.

How other tools differ

GitHub renders the GFM spec and its documented syntax adds footnotes and the five alert types; the GFM spec itself notes that GitHub also post-processes and sanitizes the HTML. Other editors each choose their own extensions and change them between releases, so the test file above is the reliable way to learn what a given tool does. For choosing an editor, see Choosing a Markdown editor for Mac.

FAQ

Is GFM the same as CommonMark?

No. GFM contains all of CommonMark and adds the extensions listed above, so a valid CommonMark note is valid GFM, but not the other way round.

Why does my table show as plain text?

The table extension needs a header row and a delimiter row with the same number of cells. An app that only implements CommonMark will never render it.

Does MiaoYan support footnotes and math?

Yes. Footnotes come from the parser, math from KaTeX in the preview. See LaTeX math in Markdown.

A daily note in Markdown is one plain file per day, named with the ISO date, such as 2026-11-14.md, kept in a folder per year. That name sorts correctly in any file browser, becomes the note title in MiaoYan, and works as a wikilink target, so one choice does three jobs. Add a short template with a date in front matter, create today's file with a few lines of shell, and rely on search for everything older. MiaoYan has no daily-note command or template setting at V4.11.0, so what follows is a convention plus a script, not a built-in feature.

Name the file for the day

Use YYYY-MM-DD.md. Year first, then month, then day, each zero-padded to a fixed width, means alphabetical order and chronological order are the same order. Names like 14-11-2026 or Nov 14 sort by day or by month name and scatter your entries.

The shell can produce the name. date +%F prints the current date as 2026-11-14, and it works with the date that ships with macOS. For yesterday, macOS uses date -v-1d +%F, while GNU date on Linux uses date -d yesterday +%F.

In MiaoYan the note title is the file name without the extension, so 2026-11-14.md shows in the list as "2026-11-14". Nothing inside the file has to repeat it.

Put them in folders by year

One folder per year keeps every list short:

MiaoYan/
  Journal/
    2025/
      2025-12-31.md
    2026/
      2026-11-13.md
      2026-11-14.md

Month folders are possible, but they add a level you rarely need when search is one keystroke away. The local-first notes post makes the same case for a shallow library. Obsidian's Daily notes plugin supports the idea directly: its help page says a date format such as YYYY/MMMM/YYYY-MMM-DD makes the plugin create the subfolders for you.

A small template

Keep the template short enough that you never skip it:

---
date: 2026-11-14
---

## Plan

## Log

## Links

The date is redundant with the file name, which is the point: a script that reads metadata does not have to parse the name, and a note that is renamed or moved still says which day it is. MiaoYan hides a leading front matter block in the preview and in exports, while the editor still shows it; the rules are in Markdown front matter. Plan holds tasks as - [ ] items (see task lists), Log is free writing, and Links holds the day's wikilinks. If a section stays empty for a week, delete it from the template.

Create today's file from the terminal

Copy cells in Excel, Numbers or Google Sheets and the clipboard holds tab-separated text, one row per line, so pasting into a Markdown file gives you tabs, not a table. To get a pipe table, convert the text. An online generator such as tablesgenerator.com is the fastest for a one-off, Pandoc (pandoc -f csv -t gfm) suits files you convert repeatedly, and a short awk filter handles a range you just copied. Afterwards check three things: merged cells, line breaks inside cells, and any | in the data.

Why the paste is not a table

A spreadsheet is a grid, and a plain-text clipboard has no grid. A copied range becomes text with a tab between cells and a line break between rows, the same layout as a .tsv file. A Markdown table needs pipes between cells and a divider row of hyphens under the header, so the tabs stay in the file as invisible whitespace and the preview shows the numbers as a paragraph.

Some apps also put an HTML version of the range on the clipboard next to the plain text, and some editors read it. MiaoYan does, as described near the end. The practical test is to paste once and look: pipes mean the HTML path worked, tabs mean you need a converter.

Option 1: an online generator

The Markdown table page on tablesgenerator.com says you can copy cells from Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc, click the top-left cell of its grid and press Ctrl+V, and the grid grows to fit. It also imports a file through File / Import CSV or Excel file, which accepts .csv and .xlsx and lets you choose a sheet. The Markdown appears under the editor, and Copy to clipboard copies it.

The same page describes the options that change the result:

  • Alignment is set per column in the Column menu's Text align submenu, and in the output each column takes the alignment of its cell in the first row. That becomes the colons in the divider row.
  • A line break inside a cell becomes a space by default. Ticking Line breaks as <br> writes <br> instead.
  • Markdown cannot merge cells. When the page imports HTML or Markdown, merged cells are split, and it points to its HTML table generator for the merged case.
  • Compact mode leaves out the spaces that line up the columns.

For a confidential sheet, a local tool is the safer default. MiaoYan's Markdown table generator converts in your browser without sending the data anywhere, takes cells copied from Excel or Google Sheets as well as CSV and TSV files, and lines up columns that hold Chinese or Japanese.

Option 2: Pandoc

Pandoc lists csv and tsv among its input formats and gfm among its output formats. The runs below used Pandoc 3.13.

pandoc -f csv -t gfm data.csv
pandoc -f tsv -t gfm data.tsv

For a TSV with a header and two data rows the output was:

| Name  | Qty |
|-------|-----|
| Apple | 3   |
| Pear  | 12  |

Export the sheet as CSV in UTF-8 so Chinese and accented text survives. To convert what is on the clipboard instead of a file, pbpaste | pandoc -f tsv -t gfm | pbcopy works on a Mac, because pbpaste and pbcopy read and write the clipboard.

Three behaviours showed up.

Pipes are escaped. A cell containing a|b came out as a\|b, so the table keeps its shape. Escaping in general is covered in Markdown escape characters.

A multi-line cell stops Pandoc writing a pipe table. With one cell containing a line break, the gfm writer produced a full HTML <table> with <br /> instead of pipes. That fits the manual's statement that pipe table cells cannot contain block elements or span multiple lines. Remove the line breaks from the cells first if you want pipes.

CJK text is padded by display width. Pandoc counts a Chinese character as two columns, so a cell holding 中文 got two fewer padding spaces than a cell holding ab, and the columns line up in a monospaced font. This only affects the raw file.

Pandoc takes the first row as the header, and the divider it writes has no alignment colons. Add :---: or ---: by hand where you want centred or right-aligned numbers.

Option 3: a command-line filter

For small tab-separated data, such as a range you just copied, this awk command escapes pipes, builds each row and adds the divider after the first line.

pbpaste | awk -F'\t' '{
  gsub(/\|/, "\\|")
  out = "|"
  for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) out = out " " $i " |"
  print out
  if (NR == 1) { s = "|"; for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) s = s " --- |"; print s }
}' | pbcopy

On a two-line sample with A|x in a cell it printed | A\|x | 3 | for the data row and | --- | --- | for the divider. It does not understand quoted CSV, so use it only on tab-separated text, and it does not pad columns, which the renderer ignores anyway.

The tricky cells

Situation What happens
Merged cells Split or lost, because pipe tables have no spans
Line break in a cell A space, <br>, or an HTML table, depending on the tool
Pipe in a cell Escaped as \| by Pandoc, the awk filter and MiaoYan
Alignment Usually lost, except in tablesgenerator.com
Header row The first row, always

The limits come from the GFM spec. The header row and divider row must have the same number of cells or the block is not a table. A body row with fewer cells gets empty cells added, extra cells are ignored, and block-level elements cannot go inside a cell.

If the sheet depends on merged cells or lists inside cells, write an HTML <table> with colspan or rowspan, or split it into two simpler tables.

Pasting a table in MiaoYan

MiaoYan has no CSV or TSV import and does not turn tab-separated text into pipes on paste. It does convert HTML. When the clipboard holds an HTML version containing a <table>, a heading, a list, a quote or a code block, the editor inserts Markdown instead of the plain text. For tables the V4.11.0 source shows this:

  • The first row always becomes the header, with th cells or without.
  • A pipe in a cell is escaped as \|.
  • A line break inside a cell becomes a space.
  • Rows shorter than the widest row are padded with empty cells on the right. The code ignores colspan, so a merged cell becomes one cell and the gap lands at the end of the row, not where the merge was.
  • The divider is plain ---, so alignment is not kept.

It is aimed at rich text copied from browsers, so whether a spreadsheet paste takes this path depends on whether the app puts HTML on the clipboard. When a paste gives you tabs, convert with Pandoc or a generator and paste the result. Markdown to HTML explains why a table sometimes shows as raw pipes in other tools.

Checking the result

Look at the rendered table, not only the source. A table that renders as a paragraph of pipes almost always has a divider row whose cell count differs from the header. A shifted column usually means an unescaped pipe in the data, and a literal <br> in a cell means the viewer escapes HTML. On a long table, check the last row and the widest row, where a stray tab or a missing cell usually shows up.

FAQ

Why does pasting from Excel give me tabs?

Spreadsheet apps copy a range as tab-separated plain text. Markdown tables use pipes, so the text needs converting first.

Can a Markdown table have merged cells?

No. Pipe tables are a plain grid. Use an HTML table with colspan or rowspan, or split the data.

How do I convert a CSV file to a Markdown table?

Run pandoc -f csv -t gfm file.csv, or import the file into a generator such as tablesgenerator.com. Remove line breaks inside cells first if you want Pandoc to write a pipe table.

cases.html:
A README is a Markdown file named README.md that GitHub shows on the front page of a repository, so it works as the project's landing page. A good one answers four things in order: what this is, how to install it, how to use it, and how to contribute. Write it in plain Markdown plus a few GitHub-friendly features, keep links and images relative so they survive branches and clones, and read it rendered before you push.

What a README is for and where GitHub shows it

GitHub's documentation lists what a README should tell a visitor: what the project does, why it is useful, how to get started, where to get help, and who maintains and contributes to it.

GitHub looks for the file in three places. If a repository has more than one README, the one displayed is chosen from the .github directory first, then the repository's root directory, and finally the docs directory. Most projects use the root, where people look first after cloning.

One limit is worth knowing: GitHub truncates README content beyond 500 KiB when it is viewed on the site, which you will only hit with embedded data.

A section order that works

This order follows what a first-time visitor asks, and MiaoYan's own README follows most of it:

  1. Name and one-line description. MiaoYan's is "A native Mac app for local Markdown notes", right under the title. Say what the thing is, not what it hopes to be.
  2. Screenshot or demo. One image under the title. MiaoYan's README has a single picture of the app on Mac, iPad and iPhone directly below the badges.
  3. Features. Three to five bullets, each a fact. "Notes are Markdown files in a folder you choose" tells a reader more than "powerful and flexible".
  4. Install. Numbered when there are several routes. The MiaoYan README lists the App Store, Homebrew and GitHub Releases, with brew install --cask miaoyan in a code block.
  5. Usage. The shortest working example, in a fenced code block. For a command-line tool, show real commands; for an app, show the one shortcut a new user needs.
  6. Configuration. Only the options people actually change, with defaults.
  7. Contributing. How to report a bug or send a patch, or a link to CONTRIBUTING.md.
  8. License. One line, such as "MIT License", matched by a LICENSE file.

Skip sections that have nothing to say, and if one grows past a screen, move it to a file under docs/ and link to it.

Code goes in fenced blocks with a language tag, so GitHub highlights it. The fence rules, including longer fences for nested code, are in Markdown code blocks.

Relative links and images

Point to files in your own repository with relative paths. GitHub's documentation says it transforms a relative link or image path based on the branch you are currently on, so the link keeps working on a feature branch, and it notes that relative links are easier for people who clone the repository. A link that starts with / is relative to the repository root.

![Split editor and preview](docs/images/split.png)
See [the syntax guide](docs/syntax.md) and [contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md).

Absolute links to your own files, such as a full github.com/.../blob/main/... URL, are a trap: they pin the file to one branch and may not work in a clone. Keep link text on a single line, as GitHub's docs ask.

MiaoYan's README does use an absolute URL for its main screenshot, hosted on the project website. That is a choice, not a rule: a hosted image still loads where the README is copied outside the repository, where a relative path may not resolve. If you publish the README in several places, hosted images are safer; if it lives on GitHub only, relative paths are simpler. Image syntax, alt text and sizing are in Markdown images, and heading anchors for deep links are in Markdown links and anchors.

When the README has several translations, link them from the top. MiaoYan's README has one line of language links, each pointing to a sibling file such as README_CN.md.

Badges

A badge is a small image, usually from shields.io, that shows a status next to the title: downloads, build state, a license, the platform. Shields.io describes itself as "concise, consistent, and legible badges", and its site shows a static badge as a URL of the form https://img.shields.io/badge/any%20text-you%20like-blue, with text, a second text segment and a colour after /badge/.

![macOS 12.0+](https://img.shields.io/badge/macOS-12.0%2B-orange?style=flat-square)

MiaoYan's README uses that badge URL, written there as an HTML <img> tag, with flat-square as a style parameter. Keep badges to the few a visitor would act on, since a long row is noise. For anything beyond the static form, read shields.io's own documentation, because the URL formats for live badges differ by service.

The outline GitHub generates

For rendered Markdown files, GitHub automatically generates a table of contents from the section headings. A visitor opens it from the Outline menu icon in the top corner of the rendered page. Two consequences follow. You do not need to maintain a hand-written table of contents in a README, and your heading hierarchy now doubles as navigation, so use ## for sections and ### for sub-sections without skipping levels. Each heading also has a link icon on hover that gives its anchor for linking straight to a section.

GitHub-specific Markdown that will not render elsewhere

GitHub Flavored Markdown covers tables, task lists, strikethrough and autolinks, and plenty of renderers support those. Several things people use in READMEs are GitHub features, not standards, and show up as raw text in viewers that do not support them. The split between the standard and the extras is in CommonMark vs GFM.

  • Alerts. A blockquote whose first line is > [!NOTE], with TIP, IMPORTANT, WARNING and CAUTION as the other types, renders with a colour and icon on GitHub. The docs advise one or two per article, not consecutively, and they cannot be nested inside other elements. Elsewhere you may see an ordinary quote starting with [!NOTE].
  • Mermaid diagrams. A fenced code block with the mermaid language is drawn as a diagram. GitHub says rendering is available in issues, discussions, pull requests, wikis and Markdown files. Tools without Mermaid support show a plain code block. See Mermaid diagrams in Markdown.
  • Issue references in task lists. A task list is - [ ] and - [x] items, and GitHub's docs show references to issues inside task items rendered as issue titles. That substitution is GitHub's; the checkboxes themselves are portable.
  • Line breaks. In issues and pull requests GitHub turns a newline into a line break, but in a .md file you need two trailing spaces, a backslash or <br/>. A README that looks right in a comment box can run together in the file.

If the README will also be read elsewhere, test it there.

Check it before you push

A README breaks in small ways: a table whose delimiter row has a different number of cells from the header, which then falls back to plain text, a wrong relative path, an unclosed code fence that swallows the rest of the page. Preview the file before GitHub shows you these.

In MiaoYan, open the README as a note and press ⌘\ to toggle the split view, with the Markdown and the rendered page side by side. Per its V4.11.0 source, the preview uses the cmark-gfm parser with tables, footnotes, strikethrough, task lists and autolinks enabled, renders Mermaid, and passes raw HTML through, so the centred <div> and <img width="..."> patterns in many READMEs show up as written. It also converts > [!NOTE] style quotes into styled callouts like GitHub's. It cannot check what depends on GitHub itself: relative links resolve against the branch you push, shields.io badges need a network connection, and the Outline menu only exists on github.com. After pushing, open the repository page once to confirm.

Any local Markdown preview does the job; the point is to look at the rendered result before others do. If you are choosing a Mac editor for this, see choosing a Markdown editor for Mac.

FAQ

Should the file be README.md or README?

Use README.md. GitHub's README documentation only speaks of a README file, but the .md extension is what tells GitHub and editors to treat it as Markdown.

How long should a README be?

As long as a visitor needs to install and run the project, and no longer. Detailed guides belong in docs/ with a link.

Can I have one README per language?

Yes. Keep the main README at the root and link README_CN.md style siblings from its first lines, as MiaoYan's does.

Do alerts and Mermaid work outside GitHub?

Not everywhere. They are GitHub features, and tools that do not support them show a plain quote or code block.

cases.html:
Write inline math between single dollar signs, like $E = mc^2$, and block math between double dollar signs on their own lines. Markdown itself has no math syntax, so the app's renderer finds those delimiters and typesets the contents with a TeX engine, usually KaTeX or MathJax. In MiaoYan the engine is KaTeX 0.16.0, bundled inside the app, so formulas render without a network connection. The common failures are a dollar sign read as math, an environment that needs a wrapper, and an underscore eaten by Markdown before the engine sees it.

Inline and block math

The energy is $E = mc^2$ in the rest frame.

$$
\int_0^1 x^2 \, dx = \frac{1}{3}
$$

Inline math sits in the sentence and uses compact layout. Block math is centered on its own line with full-size operators, so sums and integrals show their limits above and below. If a formula is part of a sentence, use inline. If it should stand on its own, use a block.

MiaoYan accepts four delimiter pairs: $...$, $$...$$, \(...\) and \[...\]. The last two are the LaTeX-native forms. You can mix them, but picking one pair for inline and one for block makes notes easier to move between apps.

Constructs you will use most

You want Write
Fraction \frac{a}{b}
Square root, nth root \sqrt{x}, \sqrt[3]{x}
Superscript, subscript x^2, x_i, and braces for more than one character: x^{10}, x_{ij}
Sum with limits \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i
Integral \int_a^b f(x)\,dx
Greek letters \alpha, \beta, \pi, \Omega
Text inside math \text{if } x > 0
Limit \lim_{t \to \infty}

\frac, \sum, \int, \sqrt and \text are all listed as supported in the KaTeX documentation. The \, before dx adds a thin space, which matches how integrals are usually typeset.

Matrices, cases and aligned equations

$$
\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & x \ge 0 \\ 0 & x < 0 \end{cases}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a &= b + c \\
  &= d
\end{aligned}
$$

Use & to separate columns and \\ to end a row. KaTeX lists matrix, pmatrix, bmatrix, cases, align, aligned and others as supported environments. In MiaoYan, wrap aligned inside $$. KaTeX's auto-render extension can pick up bare \begin{align} blocks by default, but MiaoYan's delimiter list has only the four pairs above, so a bare \begin{align} is not recognized as a math block. The wrapped form works across more tools anyway.

How it actually works

A Markdown parser has no idea what a formula is. If it sees a_b_c, it may read the underscores as emphasis. If it sees \\, it may read one backslash as an escape. So an app has to protect the math before the Markdown pass, then hand the original text to the TeX engine afterwards.

MiaoYan does this in two steps. First, a pre-pass finds math ranges outside code spans and fences, ignores escaped delimiters, and shields their contents from the parser. Second, the rendered HTML loads into a web view, where KaTeX's auto-render script scans the page for the four delimiter pairs and replaces them with typeset output. KaTeX's default ignored tags include code and pre, so math inside a code fence is never rendered.

Engines also differ in speed and LaTeX coverage. KaTeX is fast and renders synchronously, but supports a subset of LaTeX. MathJax is the other common engine, and Typora's site says it supports most MathJax extensions, including mhchem and AMSmath. If your formulas come from a paper using exotic packages, test them in the editor before relying on them. MiaoYan's bundled KaTeX 0.16.0 runs entirely from files inside the app.

Dollar signs and prices

A single $ is also a currency symbol, which is the most common pitfall. MiaoYan has a guard for it: a dollar sign followed by digits and then something that is not a math continuation is treated as currency. So It costs $5 today stays text, while $2+2$ is still math, because a + after the digits counts as math. The guard stops at letters: $5M and $10M is read as one formula between the two dollars. Since V4.10.0 a backslash helps: \$5M and \$10M shows two dollar signs, because MiaoYan turns each \$ outside code and math into a dollar the math pass skips, and an inline $ pairs only with a $ in the same paragraph. In older versions, and in apps that drop the backslash before the math pass, put the amount in a code span or reword it:

The budget grew from `$5M` to 10 million dollars.

Code spans and fenced blocks are skipped by the math pass, so this looks the same in every editor.

What goes wrong and how to check

  1. Nothing renders and the dollar signs show. The closing delimiter is missing or crosses a code span. Math cannot start in a code span and end outside it.
  2. The formula is cut after an underscore. The text was read as Markdown. In MiaoYan this is already protected, but in other apps use \_ or switch to a block.
  3. A block formula stays in a paragraph with stray line breaks. Put $$ on its own lines with a blank line before and after. MiaoYan also cleans line breaks inside single-paragraph $$ blocks, and multi-line formulas render the same under either line-break setting.
  4. Unbalanced braces. Every { needs a }. The engine will not typeset a formula with unbalanced braces.
  5. A command does nothing. It may be outside KaTeX's supported list. Check the KaTeX "Supported Functions" page before assuming a bug.

To test your setup, put these three lines in a new note and open the preview with ⌘3, or split mode with ⌘\:

Inline: $\sqrt{2}$

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}
$$

Price: $5 today

If you see a root sign, a sum with limits, and a literal $5, the engine and the currency guard both work. Math also works inside MiaoYan's presentation mode, covered in Markdown to slides. For the rest of the syntax, see the Markdown cheat sheet.

Limits to know

  • KaTeX covers most of what notes need, but not all of LaTeX. Packages and macros defined with \newcommand in a preamble are not part of a Markdown note.
  • Math is rendered in the preview. The editor pane shows raw source.
  • PDF, HTML and image exports are produced from the rendered preview. Check an exported file once to verify any formulas you care about; Markdown to PDF on Mac covers the PDF route.

FAQ

Does MiaoYan need an internet connection for math?

No. KaTeX is bundled inside the app. The exception in this family of features is PlantUML, which is sent to a public server.

KaTeX or MathJax, which should I pick?

If you need a specific MathJax-only extension, use an editor that offers it. For ordinary algebra, calculus, matrices and aligned equations, KaTeX is enough and renders quickly.

How do I write a literal dollar sign?

In MiaoYan a price such as $5 followed by a space or punctuation already stays text. For anything else, such as $5M, write \$5M, which MiaoYan shows as a plain dollar sign since V4.10.0, or put it in inline code, which also works in other apps.

Can I number equations?

Typora's site says it can auto-number equations when enabled. MiaoYan has no equation numbering setting. KaTeX supports \tag{1} on lines in some environments, which gives you manual labels.
